<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="179cc0cf-4aff-5dd9-80cb-c4bbf21c5442" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/41/uconn-huskies">UConn Huskies</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> Oct. 21, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> Vukosa is a 6-foot-4 versatile post player from Whitestone, New York. She is also the No. 1 post player in her class in the country. She chose UConn over LSU, Texas, Ohio State and South Carolina. She is adding another name to the pipeline between UConn and Queens-based prep program Christ the King, which has sent the likes of Sue Bird and Tina Charles to Storrs.</p><p>Vukosa brings a wealth of experience via international play, having represented Croatia in FIBA competition in the 2023 U16 Women's European Championship, the 2024 Women's World Cup -- and, most recently, the 2025 U20 EuroBasket B Division, where she won a bronze medal after averaging 15.6 points and 9.1 rebounds. The highlight of her summer was a 35-point, 22-board performance in the third-place game against Bulgaria.</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Vukosa is in the mold of the traditionally multifaceted post player favored by Geno Auriemma -- in fact, she fits the mold of the prototypical UConn player with whom Auriemma has seen success over the years. UConn is very methodical about building its roster and tends to look for the next name around which to anchor its rosters: Breanna Stewart in 2012, Napheesa Collier in 2015, Paige Bueckers in 2020, <a data-player-guid="343afb44-7a8b-3984-8141-361e8045fdaa" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/4433790/azzi-fudd">Azzi Fudd</a> in 2021 and <a data-player-guid="fd94de8d-1c86-30b9-9218-b2449577013c" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5239592/sarah-strong">Sarah Strong</a> in 2024.</p><p>When it comes to Vukosa, the Huskies should be able to utilize her skill set beyond the block and the paint, as she is a competent decision-maker and passer, and has the ability to play outside the 3-point line. Think of <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/63102/stefanie-dolson">Stefanie Dolson</a>, who was a key support for Stewart during the first two years of UConn's run of four straight title wins (2013-16).</p><p>Vukosa, a true center, will allow UConn to continue running its offense through a big who lifts the opponent's defensive anchor and spaces the floor for quick, speedy playmakers. Vukosa should be able to play well off Strong and advance her effectiveness, much like Collier did with Stewart during those title runs. She should also fit well with 2025 recruit <a data-player-guid="f49f34ae-a27a-311e-9250-d5d05212fa28" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5312306/blanca-quinonez">Blanca Quiñonez</a> -- who also has comparable international experience and playing styles -- and open things up for the likes of <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/250996/kayleigh-heckel">Kayleigh Heckel</a> and <a data-player-guid="1bd4ae3c-e981-30a2-ad1b-27a6fad7ecf6" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5174491/kk-arnold">KK Arnold</a>. Vukosa has an incredibly high ceiling and could seriously challenge current No. 1 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252388/saniyah-hall">Saniyah Hall</a> by the end of this season.</p><hr><aside class="inline inline-photo full"><figure><picture><source data-srcset="https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F0809%2Fr1529662_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=570&format=jpg, https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F0809%2Fr1529662_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=1140&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(min-width: 376px)"><source data-srcset="https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F0809%2Fr1529662_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=375, https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F0809%2Fr1529662_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=750&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(max-width: 375px)"><img class=" lazyload lazyload" data-image-container=".inline-photo" height="320" width="570"></picture><figcaption class="photoCaption">Kate Harpring, No. 4 in the 2026 ESPNW 100 class, is a high-profile recruiting win for North Carolina. <cite>Courtesy of USA Basketball</cite></figcaption></figure></aside><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/153.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252399/kate-harpring">Kate Harpring</a>, PG</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking:</strong> 4<br>

<strong>Commitment date:</strong> Aug. 9, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> The Georgia native, who currently plays for Marist School, <a href="/womens-college-basketball/story/_/id/45932667/north-carolina-lands-kate-harpring-no-4-2026-espnw-100">picked the Tar Heels</a> over the likes of Iowa, South Carolina and other powerhouse programs. <script async="" src="//javascript:;"></script><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Harpring is a physical, competitive scorer who blew up last year to become a top-5 player in the class. She gives North Carolina its highest-rated recruit since No. 4 <a data-player-guid="20d3a6f6-3cd5-3337-a1c3-d33f39dbd224" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5174425/ciera-toomey">Ciera Toomey</a> in 2023. She represents the possibility of interchangeable parts with current freshman <a data-player-guid="411bbd91-82dd-3614-b775-4f0771861576" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5311568/aaliyah-crump">Aaliyah Crump</a> and star <a data-player-guid="bea8fdf4-b5dd-3a14-bae0-b5c314cde4fe" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5175792/madison-booker">Madison Booker</a> -- all of them are forwards with guard skill who can open up the floor and guard multiple positions.</p><hr><aside class="inline inline-photo full"><figure><picture><source data-srcset="https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1017%2Fr1561669_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=570&format=jpg, https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1017%2Fr1561669_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=1140&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(min-width: 376px)"><source data-srcset="https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1017%2Fr1561669_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=375, https://a2.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1017%2Fr1561669_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=750&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(max-width: 375px)"><img class=" lazyload lazyload" data-image-container=".inline-photo" height="320" width="570"></picture><figcaption class="photoCaption">Five-star Autumn Fleary is the fourth top-50 commit for Duke in the 2026 class. <cite>Courtesy of USA Basketball</cite></figcaption></figure></aside><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/150.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252385/autumn-fleary">Autumn Fleary</a>, PG</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking:</strong> 13<br>
<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="0b5ffae8-a6ca-0e67-0cd5-81c5531527f8" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/150/duke-blue-devils">Duke Blue Devils</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> Oct. 18, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> Fleary, the top-ranked point guard in the 2026 class, picked Duke over LSU, North Carolina and UCLA. She is the fourth top-50 -- and second five-star commit this week -- for Duke.</p><p>The 5-foot-7 Fleary had a big summer, leading her Team Takeover squad to the Nike EYBL Championship in July and averaging 19.1 points, 3.4 rebounds, and 3.1 assists. She is also a key member of perennial top-10 team Sidwell Friends (DC).</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Fleary is a true point guard in every sense of the word the way she handles the ball, breaks down defenders in the pick and roll game and, most importantly, wins. Fleary is the fourth top 50 commit in the class and the second 5-star commit this week for Kara Lawson and the Blue Devils. She and No. 16 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252386/bella-flemings">Bella Flemings</a>, who announced her commitment Monday, join No. 25 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252387/sanai-green">Sanai Green</a> and No. 43 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/260940/taylor-sofilkanich">Taylor Sofilkanich</a> in what is now a top 5 recruiting class in the country.</p><p>This group consists of a true point guard (Fleary), two strong interchangeable guards (Flemings and Green) and a post anchor (Sofilkanich). Projecting Final Four expectations for Duke's lineup of the future -- which includes guard <a data-player-guid="6f3d3737-4dea-337c-8650-81dc552e6551" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5311970/emilee-skinner">Emilee Skinner</a> of the 2025 class and redshirt freshman <a data-player-guid="3543886a-12b2-326a-8c4b-455bc5836490" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5238276/arianna-roberson">Arianna Roberson</a>, plus the sophomore class of <a data-player-guid="812519ed-49c2-3e32-adec-1b0a5704dc02" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5238277/toby-fournier">Toby Fournier</a> and <a data-player-guid="066621e8-5a09-3516-9d50-a318b10f578b" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/4894357/riley-nelson">Riley Nelson</a> -- is not far-fetched.</p><p>Fleary will be a fantastic replacement for senior guard <a data-player-guid="db8bf392-38a2-3c5b-8437-df665ff5cdfe" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5106222/taina-mair">Taina Mair</a> for a Duke team that lost in the Elite 8 last year to South Carolina by four points. Her defensive prowess, particularly on the ball with the ability to pick up 94 feet, is perfect for the Duke system.</p><hr><img alt="" class="floatleft imageLoaded" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/96.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/254715/maddyn-greenway">Maddyn Greenway</a>, PG</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 ranking:</strong> 14<br>
<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="7b8166a0-b6df-d465-7e16-64d5933ba54c" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/96/kentucky-wildcats">Kentucky Wildcats</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> Nov. 16, 2024</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> The 5-foot-8 multisport athlete (basketball, soccer, track) chose Kentucky over finalists Iowa, Duke, Clemson, UCLA, and Stanford in November. It was a massive win for Wildcats coach Kenny Brooks, who has two top-20 commits (No. 18 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/254716/savvy-swords">Savvy Swords</a>).</p><p>Greenway is one of the most decorated high school players to come out of Minnesota. She won state championships in all three sports, and just earned a gold medal with the 2025 USA Women's Basketball U19 World Cup team. She's also the reigning Minnesota Gatorade Player of the Year. Her mother, Jenni, ran track at Iowa (and is her high school track coach), and her father, Chad, played 11 years in the NFL after starring at linebacker for the Hawkeyes.</p><blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Five-star Michigan State commit <a href="https://twitter.com/LillyAWilliams?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@LillyAWilliams</a> is getting it done on both ends at Super Showcase 🔥<a href="https://twitter.com/MImystics?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@MImystics</a> <a href="https://t.co/OmxUpVMTqZ">pic.twitter.com/OmxUpVMTqZ</a></p>— Select Events Basketball (@SelectEventsBB) <a href="https://twitter.com/SelectEventsBB/status/1943416664965722272?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 10, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async="" src="//javascript:;" charset="utf-8"></script><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Kentucky's point guards must be major playmakers, and Greenway provides that. She puts immediate pressure on the defense and scores at all three levels. She's the ultimate competitor defensively, applying ball pressure and all-out hustle in rotations.</p><p><strong>What's next:</strong> Greenway will be tasked with becoming the next star point guard for Brooks, much like Georgia Amoore, who led Virginia Tech to a Final Four with him as coach in 2023 before both moved to Kentucky. Brooks is hoping to build Kentucky similarly in Year 2.</p><hr><aside class="inline inline-photo full"><figure><picture><source data-srcset="https://a3.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1031%2Fr1568928_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=570&format=jpg, https://a3.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1031%2Fr1568928_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=1140&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(min-width: 376px)"><source data-srcset="https://a3.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1031%2Fr1568928_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=375, https://a3.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1031%2Fr1568928_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=750&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(max-width: 375px)"><img class=" lazyload lazyload" data-image-container=".inline-photo" height="320" width="570"></picture><figcaption class="photoCaption">Olivia Jones is the second five-star commitment for coach Shea Ralph at Vanderbilt, following No. 8 Mikayla Blakes in 2024. <cite>Courtesy of USA Basketball</cite></figcaption></figure></aside><img alt="" class="floatleft imageLoaded" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/238.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/260957/olivia-jones">Olivia Jones</a>, G</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking:</strong> 16<br>

<strong>Commitment Date:</strong> Oct. 31, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> Jones is a 5-foot-11 guard from Long Island Lutheran in New York. She will also be eligible for the U17 team after she graduates high school as she is particularly young for her grade and could technically be in the class of 2027.</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Vanderbilt's current headliner is sophomore guard <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/244046/mikayla-blakes">Mikayla Blakes</a>. Jones and Blakes will be a nice complementary duo for a couple seasons at Vanderbilt. They play a fast-paced read-and-react style under Shea Ralph. Jones and Blakes are expected to be dedicated defenders, and they have the opportunity to be aggressive offensively.</p><p>Vandy is still in the hunt for No. 35 <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/266629/jhai-johnson">Jhai Johnson</a> (California) and a physical four-star Sther Ubaka out of DME in Florida.</p><hr><img alt="" class="floatleft imageLoaded" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/127.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/260953/lilly-williams">Lilly Williams</a>, P</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 ranking:</strong> 17<br>

<strong>Commitment date:</strong> Feb. 4, 2024</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> Williams' path to becoming one of the top post players in the country was different from many on this list: She was homeschooled until this upcoming season (where she will attend Howell High School in Michigan), and she played for an independent club program, the Michigan Mystics P24, rather than for a shoe circuit team. She will join the program as the tallest player on the roster, and will be expected to anchor a defense that prides itself on pressure and creating turnovers. As a mobile and strong interior player, Williams will give the Spartans a true center to play through. The program will still look to sign a point guard and scoring guard to round out the class.</p><hr><aside class="inline inline-photo full"><figure><picture><source data-srcset="https://a1.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1013%2Fr1559723_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=570&format=jpg, https://a1.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1013%2Fr1559723_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=1140&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(min-width: 376px)"><source data-srcset="https://a1.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1013%2Fr1559723_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=375, https://a1.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1013%2Fr1559723_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=750&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(max-width: 375px)"><img class=" lazyload lazyload" data-image-container=".inline-photo" height="320" width="570"></picture><figcaption class="photoCaption">Bella Flemings, who has never fallen outside of the top 20 in the player recruiting rankings for the 2026 class, has committed to Kara Lawson and Duke. <cite>Julia Beverly/Getty Images</cite></figcaption></figure></aside><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/150.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252386/bella-flemings">Bella Flemings</a>, G</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking:</strong> 18<br>
<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="0b5ffae8-a6ca-0e67-0cd5-81c5531527f8" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/150/duke-blue-devils">Duke Blue Devils</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> October 13, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> The 6-foot guard committed to Duke over Tennessee, Baylor, TCU and Miami.</p><p>She has been a consistent presence in the top 20 rankings due to reliable play, maturity and high basketball IQ. She was an identifiable talent early, playing years above her age with her club program (UA Next's SA Finest) and has steadily sharpened her game acumen over time. This summer on the Under Armour circuit, she averaged 18.6 points, 5.4 rebounds and 3 assists at 42.2% 3-point shooting.</p><p>She is also the younger sister of Kingston Flemings, the former five-star recruit in the boys' 2025 class who will play at Houston this season.</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Kara Lawson, recently named the head coach of USA Basketball's women's national team, likes to play interchangeable guards who can both shoot and initiate offense on the perimeter. Flemings can do both.</p><p>She joins a class already consisting of No. 25 guard <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252387/sanai-green">Sanai Green</a> and No. 43 post <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/260940/taylor-sofilkanich">Taylor Sofilkanich</a>. Green is similar to Flemings, in that -- despite missing her junior year because of a knee injury -- she is a physically strong guard with impressive fundamentals. The 6-4 Sofilkanich meanwhile is effective around the rim with her old-school post game.</p><p>Combined with big lead guard <a data-player-guid="6f3d3737-4dea-337c-8650-81dc552e6551" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5311970/emilee-skinner">Emilee Skinner</a> of the 2025 class and redshirt freshman <a data-player-guid="3543886a-12b2-326a-8c4b-455bc5836490" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5238276/arianna-roberson">Arianna Roberson</a>, plus the sophomore class of <a data-player-guid="812519ed-49c2-3e32-adec-1b0a5704dc02" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5238277/toby-fournier">Toby Fournier</a> and <a data-player-guid="066621e8-5a09-3516-9d50-a318b10f578b" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/4894357/riley-nelson">Riley Nelson</a>, this 2026 trio give Duke the foundation to strongly contend for future Final Fours. Duke will have significant minutes to replace once current seniors <a data-player-guid="2892cbb6-410c-3f84-9aae-594f58242912" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5106232/ashlon-jackson">Ashlon Jackson</a> and <a data-player-guid="db8bf392-38a2-3c5b-8437-df665ff5cdfe" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5106222/taina-mair">Taina Mair</a> depart after this season; the 2026 class will help do so.</p><hr><aside class="inline inline-photo full"><figure><picture><source data-srcset="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1110%2Fr1573854_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=570&format=jpg, https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1110%2Fr1573854_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=1140&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(min-width: 376px)"><source data-srcset="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1110%2Fr1573854_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=375, https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fphoto%2F2025%2F1110%2Fr1573854_1296x729_16%2D9.jpg&w=750&cquality=40&format=jpg 2x" media="(max-width: 375px)"><img class=" lazyload lazyload" data-image-container=".inline-photo" height="320" width="570"></picture><figcaption class="photoCaption">Five-star girls' SC Next Top 100 recruit Kaeli Wynn will play for Dawn Staley at South Carolina in 2026-27. <cite>Courtesy of Kaeli Wynn</cite></figcaption></figure></aside><img alt="" class="floatleft imageLoaded" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/2579.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/260947/kaeli-wynn">Kaeli Wynn</a>, F</h2><p><strong>2026 SC Next 100 ranking:</strong> 19<br>
<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="f136e3f6-bfeb-c813-7b33-9e873ff1eda1" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2579/south-carolina-gamecocks">South Carolina Gamecocks</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> <a href="/womens-college-basketball/story/_/id/46920932/south-carolina-lands-kaeli-wynn-no-17-2026-class">Nov. 10, 2025</a></p><p><strong>Background:</strong> Wynn, the daughter of two coaches with years of collegiate experience, is the ultimate versatile hooper. She chose South Carolina over Stanford; she had been narrowed down to those two schools for some time.</p><p>With her strong 6-2 build and elite fundamental base of skills, Wynn fills a lot of holes on the floor. She missed the summer after dislocating her right knee late in the high school season, conservatively choosing to rehab versus competing on the club circuit with her Sports Academy Swish squad in the Nike EYBL. In the summer of 2024, she averaged 13.3 points, 4.2 rebounds and 2.7 assists per game on 33% shooting from beyond the arc on the circuit.</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Wynn will bring a much-needed ability to shoot the ball to South Carolina. She will be able to get on the floor in multiple spots, bringing a physicality to the wing spot as well as a versatility to the forward spot that will allow the Gamecocks to space the floor and attack the glass. She has the finer details of touch and overall fundamentals that make her a seemingly positionless player -- able to slide into a guard spot or over to the forward, depending on her team's needs. Much like current Gamecock <a data-player-guid="e84447d6-ce27-390c-9326-a2d44fee8e70" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5121055/chloe-kitts">Chloe Kitts</a>, she could be a consistent threat from deep. She joins post player <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/252379/kelsi-andrews">Kelsi Andrews</a> in the 2026 class. Together, the duo will give depth to the frontcourt of a program rich in its history of posts and forwards.</p><p>Next season, expect Wynn to combine excellently with current freshmen forwards <a data-player-guid="b75a0c88-f1eb-3ed2-b930-23ded5e6ebcc" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5311577/agot-makeer">Agot Makeer</a> and <a data-player-guid="58ea3a1c-4030-3846-a3d7-ad1eac427a27" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5311576/ayla-mcdowell">Ayla McDowell</a>. All three are essentially interchangeable defensively and can shoot the ball from deep. She should also complement program cornerstone <a data-player-guid="88ad377a-4b04-3a72-b3ee-1c39661425bf" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5239100/joyce-edwards">Joyce Edwards</a> very well for two years: The two could play well off of each other, as they both move well without the ball and have a knack for reading the floor.</p><p>Wynn also brings a brash confidence to the court and talks like a coach on the floor, whether or not she is playing. She will bring energy and bring vocal leadership to the floor every day.</p><hr><img alt="" class="floatleft imageLoaded" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/ncaa/500/96.png&w=110&h=110" width="31"><div class="ad-300"><div class="ad-center"><div class="ad-slot ad-slot-incontent2 ad-wrapper" data-slot-type="incontent2" data-slot-kvps="pos=incontent2" data-independent="true" id="ad-slot-incontent2-224079"></div></div></div><h2><a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/254716/savvy-swords">Savvy Swords</a>, W</h2><p><strong>2026 ESPNW 100 ranking:</strong> 20<br>
<strong>Committed to:</strong> <a data-clubhouse-guid="7b8166a0-b6df-d465-7e16-64d5933ba54c" href="/womens-college-basketball/team/_/id/96/kentucky-wildcats">Kentucky Wildcats</a><br>
<strong>Commitment date:</strong> June 21, 2025</p><p><strong>Background:</strong> The younger sister of Michigan guard and Canadian Olympian <a data-player-guid="a40accc6-bed2-39f2-85e3-8a5f753a5600" href="https://www.espn.com/womens-college-basketball/player/_/id/5240185/syla-swords">Syla Swords</a>, Swords is a Canadian national team staple when not playing at Long Island Lutheran (New York) in high school. She missed most of the 2024-25 high school season and summer because of a knee injury, but has rehabbed successfully. She has played with a lot of winning teams, from high school to FIBA competition. She committed to Kentucky over finalists South Carolina, UCLA, Michigan and Notre Dame.</p><p><strong>How she fits:</strong> Swords, 6-1, can log minutes at wing or forward and potentially be interchangeable with 2025 McDonald's All-American signee <a href="https://www.espn.com/high-school/girls-basketball/recruiting/player/_/id/248063/kaelyn-carroll">Kaelyn Carroll</a>. Swords is a confident shooter and facilitator from the perimeter, but plays with the physicality needed inside. She and Maddyn Greenway are a great early tandem of commits for the Wildcats.</p>

gold_standard.gold_text:
There are two five-stars left on the board in the SC Next 100 class of 2026 as the college basketball offseason gets underway: No. 3 Oliviyah Edwards and No. 11 Trinity Jones decommitted from Tennessee and Clemson, respectively, in early April. The remaining five-stars are all expected to join their respective college programs this summer.

We won't see how these top talent really perform in a college uniform until the 2026-27 season begins -- but we can make some informed projections until then. How will they fit in their chosen system? What's next for those programs that have signed these top-tier talents? We try to answer all these questions here.

Saniyah Hall, G

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 1
Committed to: USC Trojans
Commitment date: July 25, 2025

Background: Hall announced her commitment to USC on ESPN's "NBA Today." She went directly from her official visit at USC to the ESPN studios to break the news, choosing the Trojans over UCLA and North Carolina. She dominated at Montverde (Florida) last season and has transferred closer to home to Spire Academy (Geneva, Ohio) for her senior year of high school.

Hall was named the MVP of the U19 FIBA Women's World Cup held in the Czech Republic, where Team USA won gold once again. She averaged 19.9 PPG, 6.4 RPG, 2.0 APG and 2.9 SPG. She shot 52.6% from the field through the tournament, including 39.3% from behind the arc.

How she fits: Hall will join a 2026-27 roster that will include Jasmine Davidson (also on the gold medal-winning U19 squad), JuJu Watkins, and 2025 FIBA Americup Gold medalist Kennedy Smith (No. 6 in the ESPNW 100 class of 2024).

The versatility and scoring prowess of this combination will pose problems for opposing teams. The Trojans will have a WNBA/European style feel to the roster. Each of these players has a niche, but all of them can handle, score and defend at a high level. USC will look to further bolster its interior play in this 2026 class, and is targeting No. 2 recruit Oliviyah Edwards, who visited campus officially earlier in the year.

How Hall must adjust: Hall has enough talent to contribute immediately -- there was even talk of her possibly reclassifying into the 2025 class. However, she will still need to make adjustments, primarily on defense, as a wing who will likely play some at forward (like she did primarily for Team USA). Hall has been the focal point offensively for her teams -- and though that aggressiveness will serve her well at all levels, she will be joining a roster that has Watkins, arguably the best scoring guard in the country. So, Hall will need to learn how to play with other truly elite players, possibly taking some of the load off Watkins as she returns from an ACL injury.

How USC is positioning itself in the recruiting race: The signing of Hall shows just how strong of a brand the Trojans have built in recruiting, particularly after joining the Big Ten. The USC staff kept Watkins, the No. 1 recruit in 2023, close to home, had the No. 1 recruiting class in 2024, landed the No. 1 player in 2025 (Jasmine Davidson) -- and has done it again with Hall. All signs point to the Trojans being a recruiting powerhouse.

Olivia Vukosa, P

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 2
Committed to: UConn Huskies
Commitment date: Oct. 21, 2025

Background: Vukosa is a 6-foot-4 versatile post player from Whitestone, New York. She is also the No. 1 post player in her class in the country. She chose UConn over LSU, Texas, Ohio State and South Carolina. She is adding another name to the pipeline between UConn and Queens-based prep program Christ the King, which has sent the likes of Sue Bird and Tina Charles to Storrs.

Vukosa brings a wealth of experience via international play, having represented Croatia in FIBA competition in the 2023 U16 Women's European Championship, the 2024 Women's World Cup -- and, most recently, the 2025 U20 EuroBasket B Division, where she won a bronze medal after averaging 15.6 points and 9.1 rebounds. The highlight of her summer was a 35-point, 22-board performance in the third-place game against Bulgaria.

How she fits: Vukosa is in the mold of the traditionally multifaceted post player favored by Geno Auriemma -- in fact, she fits the mold of the prototypical UConn player with whom Auriemma has seen success over the years. UConn is very methodical about building its roster and tends to look for the next name around which to anchor its rosters: Breanna Stewart in 2012, Napheesa Collier in 2015, Paige Bueckers in 2020, Azzi Fudd in 2021 and Sarah Strong in 2024.

When it comes to Vukosa, the Huskies should be able to utilize her skill set beyond the block and the paint, as she is a competent decision-maker and passer, and has the ability to play outside the 3-point line. Think of Stefanie Dolson, who was a key support for Stewart during the first two years of UConn's run of four straight title wins (2013-16).

Vukosa, a true center, will allow UConn to continue running its offense through a big who lifts the opponent's defensive anchor and spaces the floor for quick, speedy playmakers. Vukosa should be able to play well off Strong and advance her effectiveness, much like Collier did with Stewart during those title runs. She should also fit well with 2025 recruit Blanca Quiñonez -- who also has comparable international experience and playing styles -- and open things up for the likes of Kayleigh Heckel and KK Arnold. Vukosa has an incredibly high CEO and could seriously challenge current No. 1 Saniyah Hall by the end of this season.

Kate Harpring, PG

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 4
Committed to: North Carolina Tar Heels
Commitment date: Aug. 9, 2025

Background: The Georgia native, who currently plays for Marist School, picked the Tar Heels over the likes of Iowa, South Carolina and other powerhouse programs. Harpring has had an exceptional year, being named MVP of the inaugural Overtime Select competition and signing an NIL deal with Adidas. She averaged 32.3 points and 10.6 rebounds during her junior year and 19.0 points, 6.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists for her Adidas 3SSB team Southeast All Stars.

Also a member of the women's under-19 5-on-5 team, Harpring helped Team USA to a gold medal at the FIBA U19 Women's World Cup, averaging 8.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists in seven games. Her father, Matt, was Mr. Georgia and starred for Marist and Georgia Tech in the 1990s. He was a first-team All-ACC selection three times before an 11-year career in the NBA -- including seven with the Utah Jazz. Kate has already broken some of her father's high school scoring records. Her brother Luke currently plays football at Georgia Tech.

How she fits: Harpring is a physical, competitive scorer who blew up last year to become a top-5 player in the class. She gives North Carolina its highest-rated recruit since No. 4 Ciera Toomey in 2023. The Tar Heels have now filled a hole in their perimeter with Harpring, who will slot into the guard spot well with her rebounding and hard-nosed defense as well as multifaceted scoring. She should easily take on the role once played by the likes of Lexi Donarski and Indya Nivar and should complement point guard Lanie Grant and wing Nyla Brooks very well next fall.

After losing out on No. 1 Saniyah Hall, the Tar Heels will build around Harpring and hope for another solid recruiting class to follow the fifth-ranked 2025 group (headlined by Brooks).

They've already gotten a head start, landing No. 48 Irene Guiamatsia on Friday night: a 6-4 forward and an active athlete around the rim who challenges shots defensively and carves out space for rebounds. Guiamatsia, who has shown considerable improvement this summer in her touch around the rim and beyond, is a lot like Maria Gakdeng, who just graduated from UNC.

Jerzy Robinson, G

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 6
Committed to: South Carolina Gamecocks
Commitment Date: Dec. 23, 2025

Background: The most physical guard in her class, Robinson chose South Carolina over LSU in the end.

The 6-foot Robinson transferred from Desert Vista (Arizona) to the storied Sierra Canyon (California) before her sophomore season. She helped Team USA win gold at the 2023 U16 AmeriCup, 2024 FIBA U17 World Cup and 2025 FIBA U19 World Cup, leading the 2023 and 2024 teams in scoring to earn MVP honors at both events.

She bullies her way to the rim and has enough handle to create her own shot, including from the perimeter. She rebounds well for a guard and doesn't back down from any matchup.

How she fits: Expect Robinson to contribute defensively and on the glass right away. The pressure she'll put on the paint by driving and earning trips to the free throw line will help as well. Her style may remind Gamecock fans of Brea Beal.

Robinson joins Kaeli Wynn and Kelsi Andrews, but the gem of South Carolina's class is arguably 6-foot-4 French forward Alicia Tournebize.

McKenna Woliczko, W

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 7
Committed to: Iowa Hawkeyes
Commitment date: Oct. 1, 2025

Background: The 6-2 forward from Archbishop Mitty in California chose Iowa over South Carolina, Ohio State and USC. Before missing the majority of her junior year and the entire summer club season with a knee injury, she had a stellar campaign, leading Mitty to the Nike TOC Championship before Christmas in Phoenix. She represented Team USA at the 2023 FIBA Americas U16 Championship and the 2024 FIBA U17 World Cup, being named to the All-Star Five at both events.

McKenna is great on the glass with a never-ending motor. She does her damage in the paint, making effort plays running the rim and on second-chance offensive rebounds and putbacks. She began to show improvement in range and ability to attack the basket off the dribble before going down with the injury.

How she fits: Woliczko is the first commit from the 2026 class for Jan Jensen's Iowa team. With forwards Jada Gyamfi and Hannah Stuelke set to graduate this year, Woliczko will have a chance to get significant playing time and make an immediate impact.

Jordyn Jackson, G

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 8
Committed to: Maryland Terrapins
Commitment date: Aug. 9, 2025

Background: Jackson chose Maryland over other finalists TCU, Alabama, Miami, South Carolina and Ohio State. A strong wing player, she established herself early in high school as one of the potential stars of the 2026 class. She has seen national success at perennial top-five program Sidwell Friends, but on July 15 announced she was transferring to the St. James Academy, following Tamika Dudley, her high school and club head coach.

Jackson solidified her five-star status this past calendar year after adding advanced handle and shooting skills, as well as nuance to her change of pace. She is an explosive high-level defender and rebounder, and now that she's more skilled with the ball in her hands, she has made her slashing physical style to the rim that much harder to guard. She most recently averaged 15.0 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists at July's Nike Nationals in Chicago.

How she fits: Maryland plays an up-tempo and aggressive scoring style. ESPN recently compared Jackson to Maryland's Kaylene Smikle because of their similar size, build and scoring ability. Smikle will graduate this school year, so Jackson can step right in to fill that void in 2026-27. She will fit nicely with returners Kyndal Walker (PG), Oluchi Okananwa (G) and shooter Rainey Welson (G).

Jackson is also Maryland's first commit of the 2026 class, so coach Brenda Frese will now look to bolster the interior, and perhaps the right combo type of guard to complement those players.

Jacy Abii, W

2026 SC Next 100 Ranking: 9
Committed to: Notre Dame Fighting Irish
Commitment date: Oct. 4, 2025

Background: Abii, 6-2, is a new-age forward who can both initiate the offense but also bang inside and control the glass. She chose Notre Dame over finalists Texas, Tennessee, UCLA and LSU.

Although she missed her junior high school season and the majority of the club season after suffering an ACL injury last summer on the Overtime Select circuit, she showed signs of being her old self late this summer. She is an excellent passer with advanced court vision and has a stroke from beyond the 3-point line. Before transferring to Legion Prep, Abii led her Frisco Liberty program to back-to-back state championships as a freshman and sophomore.

How she fits: Abii gives Notre Dame its third commitment in the 2026 class. The Fighting Irish have landed No. 30 Isabella Ragone, a small forward out of Georgia, and No. 81 Isabella Sangha, a power forward out of Florida. Abii bolsters an already strong frontcourt class, with a unique combination of versatility and physicality. Notre Dame retooled its roster for this season via the transfer portal, but will be guard-heavy when the 2026 class arrives on campus, leaving ample opportunity for minutes and contribution at the forward spot.

Addison Bjorn, W

2026 SC Next 100 ranking: 10
Committed to: Texas Longhorns
Commitment date: November 20, 2025

Background: The 6-foot-1 wing chose the Longhorns over Iowa, North Carolina, UConn, Kansas, Notre Dame, and Duke.

Bjorn is a three-time gold medallist with Team USA, having participated in the 2025 Women's U19 World Cup, the 2024 Women's U17 World Cup and the 2023 Women's U16 AmeriCup. On the Nike EYBL circuit this spring, she averaged 17.6 points, 5.3 rebounds, and 3.1 assists for All Iowa Attack, on an efficient 65% shooting from the field overall.

Bjorn has an advanced handle for her build as a long and lanky traditional wing. She has improved her ability to pull up off the bounce and her willingness to shoot 3s over the past two summers.

How she fits: What may stand out the most about Bjorn is her adaptability -- she has proven to be able to be the focal point of an offense, but when the game calls for it play an elite supporting role. This translates very well from high school to college and beyond. Her ability to guard multiple positions with her length and toughness will help her get on the court early next year, very important in the Texas program.

She will bring an interchangeable piece that will pair well with current freshman Aaliyah Crump and star Madison Booker as well as fellow 2026 top-10 commitment, Brihanna Crittendon. Bjorn's offensive skill will allow the Longhorns to play faster and spread the floor for the future with shifty guard Aaliah Spaight also joining next season -- and as current speedy sophomore guard Bryanna Preston presumably takes more of the ballhandling responsibilities. Overall, Bjorn solidifies Texas as one of the top recruiting classes in college women's basketball.

Brihanna Crittendon, W

2026 SC Next 100 ranking: 12
Committed to: Texas Longhorns
Commitment date: November 19, 2025

Background: The 6-3 Crittendon is the quintessential face up forward in today's game. She chose Texas over Tennessee, TCU, Colorado, Oregon, Washington, Ohio State and UCLA.

She is long, agile and hunts shots from beyond the arc. This summer with her Jason Kidd Select squad on the Power 24 circuit, she showed a dedication to the glass and on the defensive end. That competitive effort coupled with her scoring ability made her a summer stock riser in the class. In her junior season at Riverdale Ridge (Colo.), she averaged 26.4 points, 5.9 rebounds, and 2.7 assists on 57% FG, 33% 3FG, and 73% FT.

How she fits: Stylistically, Crittendon will give Texas a sharp-shooting forward who fits with other talented scoring options. She will come in with a class that includes dynamic guard Aaliah Spaight (SC Next 100 No. 20) and sharpshooting guard Amalia Holguin (SC Next 100 No. 57). Texas always has size, and in this case will add versatile size and skill in Crittendon. She represents the possibility of interchangeable parts with current freshman Aaliyah Crump and star Madison Booker -- all of them are forwards with guard skill who can open up the floor and guard multiple positions.

Autumn Fleary, PG

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 13
Committed to: Duke Blue Devils
Commitment date: Oct. 18, 2025

Background: Fleary, the top-ranked point guard in the 2026 class, picked Duke over LSU, North Carolina and UCLA. She is the fourth top-50 -- and second five-star commit this week -- for Duke.

The 5-foot-7 Fleary had a big summer, leading her Team Takeover squad to the Nike EYBL Championship in July and averaging 19.1 points, 3.4 rebounds, and 3.1 assists. She is also a key member of perennial top-10 team Sidwell Friends (DC).

How she fits: Fleary is a true point guard in every sense of the word the way she handles the ball, breaks down defenders in the pick and roll game and, most importantly, wins. Fleary is the fourth top 50 commit in the class and the second 5-star commit this week for Kara Lawson and the Blue Devils. She and No. 16 Bella Flemings, who announced her commitment Monday, join No. 25 Sanai Green and No. 43 Taylor Sofilkanich in what is now a top 5 recruiting class in the country.

This group consists of a true point guard (Fleary), two strong interchangeable guards (Flemings and Green) and a post anchor (Sofilkanich). Projecting Final Four expectations for Duke's lineup of the future -- which includes guard Emilee Skinner of the 2025 class and redshirt freshman Arianna Roberson, plus the sophomore class of Toby Fournier and Riley Nelson -- is not far-fetched.

Fleary will be a fantastic replacement for senior guard Taina Mair for a Duke team that lost in the Elite 8 last year to South Carolina by four points. Her defensive prowess, particularly on the ball with the ability to pick up 94 feet, is perfect for the Duke system.

Maddyn Greenway, PG

2026 ESPNW 100 ranking: 14
Committed to: Kentucky Wildcats
Commitment date: Nov. 16, 2024

Background: The 5-foot-8 multisport athlete (basketball, soccer, track) chose Kentucky over finalists Iowa, Duke, Clemson, UCLA, and Stanford in November. It was a massive win for Wildcats coach Kenny Brooks, who has two top-20 commits (No. 18 Savvy Swords).

Greenway is one of the most decorated high school players to come out of Minnesota. She won state championships in all three sports, and just earned a gold medal with the 2025 USA Women's Basketball U19 World Cup team. She's also the reigning Minnesota Gatorade Player of the Year. Her mother, Jenni, ran track at Iowa (and is her high school track coach), and her father, Chad, played 11 years in the NFL after starring at linebacker for the Hawkeyes.

How she fits: Kentucky's point guards must be major playmakers, and Greenway provides that. She puts immediate pressure on the defense and scores at all three levels. She's the ultimate competitor defensively, applying ball pressure and all-out hustle in rotations.

What's next: Greenway will be tasked with becoming the next star point guard for Brooks, much like Georgia Amoore, who led Virginia Tech to a Final Four with him as coach in 2023 before both moved to Kentucky. Brooks is hoping to build Kentucky similarly in Year 2.

Olivia Jones, G

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 16
Committed to: Vanderbilt Commodores
Commitment Date: Oct. 31, 2025

Background: Jones is a 5-foot-11 guard from Long Island Lutheran in New York. She chose Vanderbilt over Miami, North Carolina and Maryland. She is one of the preeminent guards of the Northeast, having played for Exodus in the Nike EYBL. She won a gold medal with Team USA in the U16 FIBA AmeriCup over the summer, averaging 8.0 points, 3.8 assists, 3.3 rebounds and 2.2 steals. She will also be eligible for the U17 team after she graduates high school as she is particularly young for her grade and could technically be in the class of 2027.

How she fits: Vanderbilt's current headliner is sophomore guard Mikayla Blakes. Jones is a similar player in terms of her development: Both burst onto the scene as talented, quick guards who refined their fundamental skill over time, transforming into some of the best in the nation in their respective classes. Jones and Blakes will be a nice complementary duo for a couple seasons at Vanderbilt. They play a fast-paced read-and-react style under Shea Ralph. Jones and Blakes are expected to be dedicated defenders, and they have the opportunity to be aggressive offensively.

Vandy is still in the hunt for No. 35 Jhai Johnson (California) and a physical four-star Sther Ubaka out of DME in Florida.

Lilly Williams, P

2026 ESPNW 100 ranking: 17
Committed to: Michigan State Spartans
Commitment date: Feb. 4, 2024

Background: Williams' path to becoming one of the top post players in the country was different from many on this list: She was homeschooled until this upcoming season (where she will attend Howell High School in Michigan), and she played for an independent club program, the Michigan Mystics P24, rather than for a shoe circuit team. She is not only good now, but has more potential to reach: At 6-foot-5, Williams can dunk.

How she fits: Williams committed to Michigan State in early 2024. She had offers from most of the Big Ten, and then some. She will join the program as the tallest player on the roster, and will be expected to anchor a defense that prides itself on pressure and creating turnovers. As a mobile and strong interior player, Williams will give the Spartans a true center to play through. The program will still look to sign a point guard and scoring guard to round out the class.

Bella Flemings, G

2026 ESPNW 100 Ranking: 18
Committed to: Duke Blue Devils
Commitment date: October 13, 2025

Background: The 6-foot guard committed to Duke over Tennessee, Baylor, TCU and Miami.

She has been a consistent presence in the top 20 rankings due to reliable play, maturity and high basketball IQ. She was an identifiable talent early, playing years above her age with her club program (UA Next's SA Finest) and has steadily sharpened her game acumen over time. This summer on the Under Armour circuit, she averaged 18.6 points, 5.4 rebounds and 3 assists at 42.2% 3-point shooting.

She is also the younger sister of Kingston Flemings, the former five-star recruit in the boys' 2025 class who will play at Houston this season.

How she fits: Kara Lawson, recently named the head coach of USA Basketball's women's national team, likes to play interchangeable guards who can both shoot and initiate offense on the perimeter. Flemings can do both.

She joins a class already consisting of No. 25 guard Sanai Green and No. 43 post Taylor Sofilkanich. Green is similar to Flemings, in that -- despite missing her junior year because of a knee injury -- she is a physically strong guard with impressive fundamentals. The 6-4 Sofilkanich meanwhile is effective around the rim with her old-school post game.

Combined with big lead guard Emilee Skinner of the 2025 class and redshirt freshman Arianna Roberson, plus the sophomore class of Toby Fournier and Riley Nelson, this 2026 trio give Duke the foundation to strongly contend for future Final Fours. Duke will have significant minutes to replace once current seniors Ashlon Jackson and Taina Mair depart after this season; the 2026 class will help do so.

Kaeli Wynn, F

2026 SC Next 100 ranking: 19
Committed to: South Carolina Gamecocks
Commitment date: Nov. 10, 2025

Background: Wynn, the daughter of two coaches with years of collegiate experience, is the ultimate versatile hooper. She chose South Carolina over Stanford; she had been narrowed down to those two schools for some time.

With her strong 6-2 build and elite fundamental base of skills, Wynn fills a lot of holes on the floor. She missed the summer after dislocating her right knee late in the high school season, conservatively choosing to rehab versus competing on the club circuit with her Sports Academy Swish squad in the Nike EYBL. In the summer of 2024, she averaged 13.3 points, 4.2 rebounds and 2.7 assists per game on 33% shooting from beyond the arc on the circuit.

How she fits: Wynn will bring a much-needed ability to shoot the ball to South Carolina. She will be able to get on the floor in multiple spots, bringing a physicality to the wing spot as well as a versatility to the forward spot that will allow the Gamecocks to space the floor and attack the glass. She has the finer details of touch and overall fundamentals that make her a seemingly positionless player -- able to slide into a guard spot or over to the forward, depending on her team's needs. Much like current Gamecock Chloe Kitts, she could be a consistent threat from deep. She joins post player Kelsi Andrews in the 2026 class. Together, the duo will give depth to the frontcourt of a program rich in its history of posts and forwards.

Next season, expect Wynn to combine excellently with current freshmen forwards Agot Makeer and Ayla McDowell. All three are essentially interchangeable defensively and can shoot the ball from deep. She should also complement program cornerstone Joyce Edwards very well for two years: The two could play well off of each other, as they both move well without the ball and have a knack for reading the floor.

Wynn also brings a brash confidence to the court and talks like a coach on the floor, whether or not she is playing. She will bring energy and bring vocal leadership to the floor every day.

Savvy Swords, W

2026 ESPNW 100 ranking: 20
Committed to: Kentucky Wildcats
Commitment date: June 21, 2025

Background: The younger sister of Michigan guard and Canadian Olympian Syla Swords, Swords is a Canadian national team staple when not playing at Long Island Lutheran (New York) in high school. She missed most of the 2024-25 high school season and summer because of a knee injury, but has rehabbed successfully. She has played with a lot of winning teams, from high school to FIBA competition. She committed to Kentucky over finalists South Carolina, UCLA, Michigan and Notre Dame.

How she fits: Swords, 6-1, can log minutes at wing or forward and potentially be interchangeable with 2025 McDonald's All-American signee Kaelyn Carroll. Swords is a confident shooter and facilitator from the perimeter, but plays with the physicality needed inside. She and Maddyn Greenway are a great early tandem of commits for the Wildcats.

Wright</span></div></h2></li></ul><div class="button button-alt sm btn-related">2 Related</div></aside><p><a href="https://official.nba.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2025/10/2025-26-NBA-Concussion-Summary.pdf">Under the NBA's concussion protocol guidelines</a>, a player cannot return to full participation for 48 hours after the time of the injury but can resume gradual activity after 24 hours as long as symptoms don't worsen. The player must hit several benchmarks while being symptom-free before he is cleared to play. He will then require clearance from the team doctor in consultation with the league protocol director.</p><p>Game 3 is Friday in Portland.</p><p>Wembanyama's spill came as he was driving to the basket with 8:57 left in the second quarter with <a data-player-guid="6694d3e6-7257-f217-35dc-f6911488b9f1" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3995/jrue-holiday">Jrue Holiday</a> defending. Wembanyama landed chin first on the court and appeared to knock himself out, with his eyes closing briefly.</p><p><a data-player-guid="d8fd1989-052d-3e45-91f2-6fda54fa5c8e" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/5037871/dylan-harper">Dylan Harper</a>, <a data-player-guid="bf077b0c-98d4-3009-bb34-a07e5a64f4d2" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/5061568/carter-bryant">Carter Bryant</a> and <a data-player-guid="2a44393f-f19d-019e-fc9a-3153d1ff0197" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/6578/harrison-barnes">Harrison Barnes</a> immediately rushed over to check on Wembanyama, along with <a data-player-guid="26c7892b-12d0-3b1d-9645-f881921a1a20" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4845367/stephon-castle">Stephon Castle</a>.</p><p>The 7-foot-4 Wembanyama sat underneath the basket for several minutes as the Spurs called a timeout and "Wemby" chants from the crowd filled Frost Bank Center. He eventually popped up and ran through the tunnel toward the locker room, with head athletic trainer Will Sevening following.</p><aside class="inline float-r inline-track"><h2 class="img-title">2026 NBA postseason</h2><img data-lazyload="true" data-src="https://a.espncdn.com/photo/2026/0412/nba_playoffs_mega_preview_cr_16x9.jpg" class="round lazyload"><p>ESPN has you covered from the play-in tournament through the 2026 NBA Finals.</p><p>• <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/48419498/nba-playoffs-2026-play-finals-schedule-scores-news-highlights-bracket-dates?referrer=scribe">Bracket, schedule, news and highlights</a><br>

So that's a good sign."</p><p>Holiday was whistled for a non-shooting foul on the play, and the Spurs subbed in backup center <a data-player-guid="7a7e5cbb-0808-0a11-08e4-5b50144abcb9" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3064560/luke-kornet">Luke Kornet</a> for Wembanyama.</p><p>"I got the foul call," Holiday said. "I didn't think I touched him, but I don't really know. After they called the foul, I went to complain to the ref. I didn't really see [Wembanyama's fall]."</p><p>A little more than 15 minutes later, Sevening returned to the Spurs bench while Wembanyama remained in the locker room. The Spurs ruled him out, saying he was in the concussion protocol.</p><p>Wembanyama had five points and four rebounds before exiting. He left the arena before the conclusion of the game, according to a team spokesperson.</p><p>"We're hoping for the best, but I haven't heard anything," forward <a data-player-guid="691dfac0-35e1-b597-c503-f0211c8f7f6f" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4395723/keldon-johnson">Keldon Johnson</a> said. "Obviously, it's a big hit that we don't have the big fellow. But we're a good team, and we'll continue to stay together, have each other's back and do what got us here."</p><div class="ad-300"><div class="ad-center"><div class="ad-slot ad-slot-incontent2 ad-wrapper" data-slot-type="incontent2" data-slot-kvps="pos=incontent2" data-independent="true" id="ad-slot-incontent2-752784"></div></div></div><p>Wembanyama, 22, became the youngest NBA Defensive Player of the Year on Monday and the first player to win the award unanimously. He averaged a career-high 25.0 points, 11.5 rebounds, 3.1 assists, 3.1 blocks and a steal per game during the regular season, becoming the only player in the NBA to tally 1,500-plus points, 700-plus rebounds, 150-plus blocks and 50-plus steals.</p><p>He produced 43 games with a block and a steal and had 50 multiblock games, which included 17 outings with five blocks or more.</p><p>In Game 1 of this series, a 111-98 Spurs win Sunday, Wembanyama had 35 points and five rebounds.</p><p>San Antonio defeated Portland in all three regular-season meetings, and Wembanyama didn't play in any of those games.</p><p>"We've played tough games without him," Castle said. "Obviously we want everybody healthy and to have him on the court. But whatever five guys are on the court [for Game 3], we're going to play like ourselves."</p>

SAN ANTONIO -- Spurs star Victor Wembanyama sustained a concussion on a hard fall during the second quarter of Tuesday night's Game 2 playoff loss to the Portland Trail Blazers.

Wembanyama played just 12 minutes before being placed in the concussion protocol and ruled out for the game.

"I just know he has a concussion and he's in the protocol," Spurs coach Mitch Johnson after the 106-103 loss, which evened the first-round series at 1. "We'll obviously take the proper and appropriate steps."

Asked if Wembanyama was being evaluated for anything beyond a concussion, Johnson added: "No."

Under the league's concussion protocol guidelines, a player cannot return to full participation for 48 hours after the time of the injury but can resume gradual activity after 24 hours as long as symptoms don't worsen. Then, the player must hit several benchmarks while being symptom-free before he is cleared to play. He'll then require clearance from the team doctor in consultation with the league protocol director.

Game 3 is Friday in Portland.

Wembanyama's spill came as he was driving to the basket with 8:57 left in the second quarter with Jrue Holiday defending. He landed chin first on the court and appeared to knock himself out, with his eyes closing briefly.

Dylan Harper, Carter Bryant and Harrison Barnes immediately rushed over to check on Wembanyama, along with Stephon Castle.

The 7-foot-4 Wembanyama sat underneath the basket for several minutes as the team called a timeout and "Wemby" chants from the crowd filled Frost Bank Center. He eventually popped up and ran through the tunnel toward the locker room, with head athletic trainer Will Sevening following.

"I was just checking on him, making sure he was OK," Castle said. "I was subbing in. Obviously, he ran off [the floor]. So, that's a good sign."

Holiday was whistled for a non-shooting foul on the play, and the Spurs subbed in backup center Luke Kornet for Wembanyama.

"I got the foul call," Holiday said. "I didn't think I touched him, but I don't really know. After they called the foul, I went to complain to the ref. I didn't really see [Wembanyama's fall]."

A little more than 15 minutes later, Sevening returned to the Spurs bench while Wembanyama remained in the locker room. The Spurs then ruled him out, saying he was in the concussion protocol.

Wembanyama had five points and four rebounds before exiting. He left the arena before the conclusion of the game, according to a team spokesperson.

"We're hoping for the best, but I haven't heard anything," forward Keldon Johnson said. "Obviously, it's a big hit that we don't have the big fellow. But we're a good team and we'll continue to stay together, have each other's back and do what got us here."

Wembanyama, 22, became the youngest NBA Defensive Player of the Year on Monday and the first player to win the award unanimously. He averaged a career-high 25.0 points, 11.5 rebounds, 3.1 assists, 3.1 blocks and a steal during the regular season, becoming the only player in the NBA to tally 1,500-plus points, 700-plus rebounds, 150-plus blocks and 50-plus steals.

Wembanyama produced 43 games with a block and a steal, and posted 50 multiblock games, which included 17 outings with five blocks or more.

In Game 1 of this series, a 111-98 Spurs win Sunday, he had 35 points and five rebounds.

San Antonio defeated Portland in all three regular-season meetings, and Wembanyama didn't play in any of those games.

"We've played tough games without him," Castle said. "Obviously we want everybody healthy and to have him on the court. But whatever five guys are on the court [for Game 3], we're going to play like ourselves."

Which stars are shining and which players are breaking through on the playoff stage?</p><p>As the <a href="/nba/story/_/id/48419498/nba-playoffs-2026-play-finals-schedule-scores-news-highlights-bracket-dates">Western Conference playoffs</a> continue, here's what matters most and what to watch in all four series.</p><p align="center"><strong>More coverage:</strong><br>

<strong>Game 2: </strong><a href="/nba/game?gameId=401869368">Thunder 120, Suns 107</a></p><p><strong>Biggest takeaway from Game 2:</strong> This win might have come at a significant cost for the Thunder.</p><p><a data-player-guid="2381f346-9247-3ba1-b632-fcef378a2799" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4593803/jalen-williams">Jalen Williams</a>, whose was off to a spectacular start in the postseason after injuries limited him to only 33 games during the regular season, exited midway through the third quarter after sustaining a left hamstring injury when he missed a contested layup on a fast break. The top-seeded Thunder went 39-10 without Williams this season, but he played a critical role during Oklahoma City's championship run a year ago, including a 40-point performance in the pivotal Game 5 of the NBA Finals.</p><p>"We're the best version of ourselves when he's the best version of himself," <a data-player-guid="4dcec409-3ff9-2881-2bc3-b4289ce6c36d" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4278073/shai-gilgeous-alexander">Shai Gilgeous-Alexander</a> said after Game 1. "We got to make sure he stays there."</p><p>Unfortunately, Williams' availability is in question as the series moves to Phoenix. -- <em>Tim MacMahon</em></p><p><strong>Game 3: </strong>Thunder at Suns (<a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869370/thunder-suns">Saturday, 3:30 p.m. ET, NBC/Peacock</a>)</p><p><strong>What to watch in Game 3:</strong> The Suns hope to get a couple of key players back with their season essentially on the line. <a data-player-guid="fedd8adf-a9cc-d643-0130-ff502fc58389" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3135045/grayson-allen">Grayson Allen</a> has yet to play in this series as he's coming off a hamstring strain, although he has been on the active roster. He's likely to get minutes Saturday afternoon.</p><p><a data-player-guid="0bd90eae-7fa2-1afb-904f-535595216bb3" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4278402/jordan-goodwin">Jordan Goodwin</a>, who opened the series as the primary defender on Gilgeous-Alexander, is dealing with soreness in the calf that he strained earlier this season. He was ruled out after warming up Wednesday. There isn't as much optimism about the potential return of starting center <a data-player-guid="93b211a2-3229-3b90-8529-f7f39ce5374d" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4701232/mark-williams">Mark Williams</a>, who has been sidelined by a foot injury that has bothered him since March. -- <em>MacMahon</em></p><hr><p><strong><strong><strong><strong><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/hou.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"></strong><strong><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/lal.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"></strong></strong></strong></strong></p><h2>(4) <a data-clubhouse-guid="2876e98b-b9bc-2920-4319-46e6943f8be4" href="/nba/team/_/name/lal/los-angeles-lakers">Los Angeles Lakers</a> lead (5) <a data-clubhouse-guid="78113ad4-1ac7-0c04-dada-388a6ff4e15e" href="/nba/team/_/name/hou/houston-rockets">Houston Rockets</a> 2-0</h2><p><strong>Game 1:</strong> <a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869190/rockets-lakers">Lakers 107, Rockets 98</a><br>
<strong>Game 2:</strong> <a href="/nba/game?gameId=401869397">Lakers 101, Rockets 94</a></p><p><strong>Biggest takeaway from Game 2: </strong>The series felt as if it changed after the first possession of Tuesday's Game 2, when <a data-player-guid="dc324fde-eee8-98e2-09ac-d31d8ad9909e" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3202/kevin-durant">Kevin Durant</a> -- out for the opener with a sore right knee -- blocked Game 1 star <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3913174/luke-kennard">Luke Kennard</a>'s shot attempt. Yet as much of an impact as Durant had -- 23 points on 6-for-9 shooting and six rebounds -- Los Angeles followed pretty much the same formula to go up 2-0:</p><p><a data-player-guid="1f6592b3-ff53-d321-8dc5-6038d48c1786" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/1966/lebron-james">LeBron James</a>, who finished with 28 points, eight rebounds and seven assists, was the best player on the court for either team. Kennard (23 points) made up for some of the offensive power missing with <a data-player-guid="583794eb-0f38-9bbd-3e25-9dd33b7f83b8" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3945274/luka-doncic">Luka Doncic</a> and <a data-player-guid="8a9d9e1c-6174-0009-4883-3b4e16b492d0" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4066457/austin-reaves">Austin Reaves</a> in street clothes. And L.A.'s defense held Houston under 100 points on just 40.4% shooting. Just to make things eerily similar to Game 1, the Lakers once again had a late-second-quarter collapse fueled by turnovers, letting the Rockets back in the game with a 12-0 run. And once again, <a data-player-guid="f5096a5b-cbc5-1d7f-d406-56c623c434e5" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/2990992/marcus-smart">Marcus Smart</a> (25 points) hit a timely fourth-quarter 3-pointer, putting L.A. up by eight with 2:23 to go. -- <em>Dave McMenamin</em></p><p><strong>Game 3:</strong> Lakers at Rockets (<a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869400/lakers-rockets">Friday, 8 p.m. ET, Prime</a>)</p><p><strong>What to watch in Game 3:</strong> After finishing the regular season 7-1 at home and going 30-11 overall at the Toyota Center, can the Rockets protect home court? Right before they went on that home surge, they suffered back-to-back losses to the visiting Lakers, on March 16 and 18. And with two days of rest between Games 2 and 3, will Durant -- who coughed up nine turnovers Tuesday -- see improvement on that knee and look even more like himself?  -- <em>McMenamin</em></p><hr><p><strong><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/sas.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"></strong><strong><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/por.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"></strong></p><h2>(2) <a data-clubhouse-guid="8aef8547-32f5-0943-a1de-e734567674cc" href="/nba/team/_/name/sa/san-antonio-spurs">San Antonio Spurs</a> tied with (7) <a href="/nba/team/_/name/por/portland-trail-blazers">Portland Trail Blazers</a> 1-1</h2><p><strong>Game 1:</strong> <a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869194/trail-blazers-spurs">Spurs 111, Trail Blazers 98</a><br>
<strong>Game 2:</strong> <a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869378/trail-blazers-spurs">Trail Blazers 106, Spurs 103</a></p><p><strong>Biggest takeaway from Game 2: </strong><a data-player-guid="0e8844b2-d923-3926-82d2-f19a29d69490" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/5104157/victor-wembanyama">Victor Wembanyama</a> took a nasty spill on a drive to the basket as <a data-player-guid="6694d3e6-7257-f217-35dc-f6911488b9f1" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3995/jrue-holiday">Jrue Holiday</a> defended with 8:57 left in the second quarter and appeared to land squarely on his chin. Wembanyama headed to the locker room several minutes later, and the team announced he had entered concussion protocol and would miss the remainder of the contest.</p><p>Wembanyama's availability is now in question with the series shifting on Friday to Portland for Games 3 and 4 after a day off Wednesday followed by a travel day on Thursday. Veteran backup <a data-player-guid="7a7e5cbb-0808-0a11-08e4-5b50144abcb9" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3064560/luke-kornet">Luke Kornet</a> is plenty capable of filling in for Wembanyama, but the club's depth takes a hit. Newcomer <a data-player-guid="058a249e-8929-5de1-5f07-4f1b4ba96a90" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/2488653/mason-plumlee">Mason Plumlee</a>, <a data-player-guid="9cfc539e-c2ed-ba99-1e28-ae92154bf09b" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/2489663/kelly-olynyk">Kelly Olynyk</a> and <a data-player-guid="c0f39624-6c78-a95d-3682-11303cd9545a" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/6427/bismack-biyombo">Bismack Biyombo</a> are viable options as backup centers, and the Spurs could opt to play rookie <a data-player-guid="bf077b0c-98d4-3009-bb34-a07e5a64f4d2" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/5061568/carter-bryant">Carter Bryant</a> at the 5 in smaller lineups. -- <em>Michael C. Wright</em></p><p><strong>Game 3: </strong>Spurs at Trail Blazers (<a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869382/spurs-trail-blazers">Friday, 10:30 p.m. ET, Prime</a>)</p><p><strong>What to watch in Game 3: </strong>The Wembanyama injury changes the dynamic, especially for San Antonio's overall team defense, and provides a sliver of hope for a scrappy Portland squad that has hung tough despite being outmanned in terms of overall talent.</p><p>It's worth noting that if Wembanyama is diagnosed with a concussion, he can't return to participation without restrictions for at least 48 hours after the time of injury and until he completes the league's required return-to-participation process. San Antonio has traditionally erred on the conservative side when bringing back players from injury, anyway. So, there's a good chance Portland will face a somewhat undermanned Spurs squad at home for Game 3. -- <em>Wright</em></p><hr><p><strong><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/min.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"><img alt="" class="floatleft" src="https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/teamlogos/nba/500/den.png&h=110&w=110" width="50"></strong></p><h2>(3) <a data-clubhouse-guid="c4aceb39-0eb9-a30b-1120-9cb5b12b677a" href="/nba/team/_/name/den/denver-nuggets">Denver Nuggets</a> tied with (6) <a data-clubhouse-guid="13f727cb-254d-b484-a337-93fcc0047add" href="/nba/team/_/name/min/minnesota-timberwolves">Minnesota Timberwolves</a> 1-1</h2><p><strong>Game 1:</strong> <a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869188/timberwolves-nuggets">Nuggets 116, Timberwolves 105</a><br>
Game 2: <a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869395/timberwolves-nuggets">Timberwolves 119, Nuggets 114</a></p><p><strong>Biggest takeaway from Game 2: </strong>The Timberwolves stole the game they needed in Denver, thanks in large part to <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3032976/rudy-gobert">Rudy Gobert</a>'s defensive work against <a data-player-guid="22f57511-06ae-1587-f01b-33965365ce0d" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3112335/nikola-jokic">Nikola Jokic</a>. Gobert -- early in the game and during several key possessions down the stretch -- made life difficult for the three-time MVP. Jokic shot 1-of-8 when guarded by Gobert, 1-of-2 in transition and 6-of-10 against everyone else.</p><div class="ad-300"><div class="ad-center"><div class="ad-slot ad-slot-incontent2 ad-wrapper" data-slot-type="incontent2" data-slot-kvps="pos=incontent2" data-independent="true" id="ad-slot-incontent2-796769"></div></div></div><p>He surged in the third quarter after Gobert went to the bench with four fouls, but Gobert returned in the fourth quarter and forced a trio of late misses that set up <a data-player-guid="cea0d1d3-6353-87c8-929e-c556ae36dc41" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3064514/julius-randle">Julius Randle</a>, <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/3934673/donte-divincenzo">Donte DiVincenzo</a> and <a data-player-guid="a2edb458-a371-3fba-ba5a-b24dd2fd2d9e" href="https://www.espn.com/nba/player/_/id/4594268/anthony-edwards">Anthony Edwards</a> to drag Minnesota over the finish line with some offensive heroics. Those three combined for 70 points, sending the series back to Minneapolis tied 1-1. -- <em>Anthony Slater</em></p><p><strong>Game 3: </strong><a href="/nba/game/_/gameId/401869398/nuggets-timberwolves">Nuggets at Timberwolves (Thursday, 9:30 p.m. ET, Amazon Prime)</a></p><p><strong>What to watch in Game 3: </strong>How will Edwards' knee continue to respond to a heavy workload series?</p><p>He missed 11 of the last 14 regular-season games for a persistent right knee issue that clearly continues to bother him. He grimaced and grabbed it at least twice in the first half. But it seemed to loosen and Edwards never needed to manage his court time.</p><p>He played a team-high 40 minutes, the most he has logged since early February. That's 78 minutes in two games for Edwards after only three games total the previous month. He wasn't hyper efficient, but he was productive and showed that elite burst when needed, finishing with 30 points, including a first-half surge that brought the Timberwolves back from an early 19-point deficit. He will get two days of rest before Thursday's Game 3. -- <em>Slater</em></p>
